# Chapter 3 — The Hill Will Teach

The wooden treehouse swayed a little in the morning air, creaking at the joints where Marcos had nailed the planks together two summers before. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] could see the blue paint peeling at the edges—not faded so much as worn, the way things get worn when they are used and loved and stood in weather. A pencil stub lay on the low window ledge, and beside it a notebook half-filled with his grandfather's careful handwriting: star names, dates, the shapes of constellations that looked nothing like their creatures until you stared at them long enough.

He had not gone down to the treehouse yet this morning. He had kept the question in his mouth since yesterday, rolling it the way he rolled the smooth stones, testing each word. He was waiting for Marcos to come through the garden, the way he did every morning, unhurried and considering.

Marcos came through the garden gate with his walking stick, moving the way he always did—each step considered, as if the ground might surprise him. The cicadas had started their song an hour earlier, and the heat had already drawn the smell of sage and rosemary up from the packed earth. His grandfather's shirt was the pale blue of old fabric, and he wore it unbuttoned at the neck.

"You are awake early," Marcos said. Not a question, but the kind of observation that waited for a response.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] turned from the treehouse. He had thought carefully about what to ask and how to ask it, the way you think when you are ten and the thing you want to know is important. He held a smooth stone in his hand without remembering he had picked one up—the grey one with the white stripe down its middle. His thumb found the stripe and traced it.

"Why does no one talk about what's on the other side of the hill?" he asked.

Marcos stopped walking. He was five paces away, between an olive tree and a patch of wild rosemary that had grown up around the base of the wall. He did not answer right away. With Marcos there was always a pause, the way there is a gap between the lightning and the sound it makes, and you can judge how far away the storm is by the count of it.

He brought his walking stick down against the ground. Once. Twice. The sound was dry and clear, like a small decisive thing, and when he looked at [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] his eyes had the same quality—direct and settled and certain.

"When I was your age," Marcos said slowly, "I went to the hill because I wanted to gather stones for building something I had planned. I spent days thinking about it, days imagining which stones would be right, where they might be, what the work would look like when it was finished. I was very certain about all of this. But the hill is not interested in your plans. I climbed up and I looked, and the stones I found were not the stones I was looking for. They were different stones. Better stones, it turned out. Stones that fit together in ways I had never imagined. Stones that the light moved through differently, that caught the sun at angles I would not have thought to look for. The hill was teaching me what I truly needed, not what I thought I needed before I climbed it. That is what I have learned from the hill over many years—that it does not lie, and it does not shout. It simply shows you what you need to know, if you are willing to see it. The hill will teach you what you need to know."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] waited, turning the stone over in his palm. But Marcos had said his piece. He stood quiet, leaning very slightly on his stick, and the cicadas sang around them both.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] nodded. He turned the grey stone slowly in his palm, watching the white stripe catch the light, then looked toward the hill.

"Are you afraid?" Marcos asked.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] started to say no. The word was right there in his mouth, ready to come out the way it always did. But Marcos was looking at him, and his grandfather did not ask questions he did not want the real answer to.

"I don't know yet," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said. "I won't know until I'm there."

Marcos nodded. He tapped his stick once more against the ground, not twice this time, just once—a period at the end of something. "That is wisdom," he said.

He turned and continued his walk through the garden, moving between the trees with the same slow consideration, and [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] did not follow. He stood where he was, with the stone in his hand and the treehouse creaking softly behind him, and felt the day open up in front of him like a path he could not yet see the end of.

The sun was high enough now that the shadows had shortened, and they would get shorter still before afternoon came. Bruno appeared in the kitchen doorway. He looked at [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and then at the hill beyond the wall, his head lifting slightly as if testing the air there. He trotted over without being called, and without waiting. The terrier circled three times around his legs, as was his habit, and settled close against his shin, his weight solid and warm.

"I know," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said to the dog, though Bruno had not spoken. "Today."

He reached down to touch Bruno's head, and the stone fell from his other hand into the dry grass. He did not pick it up. When he stood, his hands were empty. The treehouse was still there, blue paint peeling, waiting on nobody. The olive trees cast their long shadows. There was the whole morning still to come, and then the afternoon, and somewhere in that stretch of hours the path up the hill was waiting too.

His mother had corrected him on the rule: not when the sun is starting to touch the horizon, when it touches. He had time. He had all the light that was coming to him.

He stood quiet for a moment, his hands empty, and looked at the hill.
